content: Early detection of visceral leishmaniasis (VL) and HIV co-infection can lead to improved outcomes. The susceptibility of Leishmania donovani in South-East Asia to low-dose liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB) presents a unique opportunity for primary prophylaxis in asymptomatic patients co-infected with VL and HIV. This approach could potentially reduce progression to symptomatic disease and warrants further investigation. Evidence suggests that maintaining specific immunity to leishmaniasis and keeping HIV viral loads undetectable are critical factors in preventing symptomatic VL in co-infected patients. Basic research is needed to better understand the immunological interactions between VL and HIV infections, as well as the immune-modulatory effects of drugs, to improve co-infection management. Given the low certainty of current evidence, additional clinical trials on combination therapies for VL-HIV co-infection are essential. Well-designed studies are urgently required to strengthen the evidence base for treatment strategies and improve patient outcomes, particularly in field conditions in East Africa and South-East Asia. The development of more user-friendly and oral medications for VL treatment must continue, as none of the current antileishmanial drugs are free from significant toxicity. Safety remains a critical area of research, as traditional pharmacovigilance approaches provide limited information. Cohort event monitoring could offer more reliable safety data. There is no available data on the safety of miltefosine therapy beyond 28 days, and studies on the safety of long-term miltefosine treatment are necessary, especially for patients requiring extended therapy due to multiple relapses. Other interventions to enhance the efficacy of antileishmanial treatments are needed to reduce relapse rates, prevent drug resistance, and minimize toxicity. Suggested research areas include early initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), the use of combined antileishmanial therapies in various scenarios, and immune-based co-therapies. Currently, there is no clear evidence on the interaction between antiretroviral drugs and antileishmanial medications, and further research is required to establish criteria for secondary prophylaxis. Secondary prophylaxis with a drug different from the one used for the primary VL attack is generally recommended to minimize resistance risk, with clear starting and stopping criteria. This is particularly important in South-East Asia, where evidence for secondary prophylaxis is limited. Research on simpler therapeutic and prophylactic regimens for VL-HIV co-infected patients is also necessary. Social determinants of VL in HIV patients remain poorly understood, and more studies are needed to address these gaps. Given the focal distribution of VL-HIV co-infection and the challenges in accessing hard-to-reach populations, conducting research in these areas is inherently difficult. Operational and implementation research on systematic screening models for VL among HIV patients and vice versa will facilitate both research and program implementation. Scientific research to better understand the impact of VL-HIV co-infection, improve program efficiency, and reduce mortality would provide valuable insights for policymakers. Additionally, research to understand the perspectives of affected communities is crucial to reduce delays in accessing healthcare services. The World Health Organization (WHO) will make these guidelines accessible on its website, with translations into official United Nations languages relevant to VL and HIV. Hard copies will be distributed through national leishmaniasis control programs to healthcare staff involved in case management. Additional tools will be developed to support country-level implementation. The incorporation of VL into national treatment protocols and field implementation will be monitored through existing support activities and the annual WHO coordination meeting on VL. The use of these guidelines will be evaluated to determine the extent of their integration into national policies and programs. Results will be published annually in WHO reports, leishmaniasis surveillance updates in the Weekly Epidemiological Record, and country profiles in East Africa and South-East Asia where HIV and VL are co-endemic. Evaluation results and new evidence will inform future updates to the guidelines.
